title: ESA Flags Anbernic Over Retro Console Sales, Adding It to US Notorious Market List
body:
The Entertainment Software Association (ESA) has formally urged the U.S. Department of Commerce to place Chinese‑based retro‑gaming hardware manufacturer Anbernic on the government’s annual Notorious Markets list, accusing the company of facilitating large‑scale piracy by bundling illegal game libraries with its handheld consoles. The move marks the first time a hardware‑focused vendor has been singled out for inclusion on a list traditionally reserved for online storefronts and streaming services that distribute unlicensed content.

ESA’s complaint argues that Anbernic’s “Retro Game Handheld” devices, which are marketed as affordable, all‑in‑one nostalgia platforms, come pre‑loaded with extensive catalogs of copyrighted titles that have not been cleared by rights holders. By offering these “polished consumer products” that ship with illicit ROMs already installed, the trade group says Anbernic normalises hardware‑based piracy and undermines the broader effort to curb digital theft across the gaming ecosystem. The association has submitted detailed evidence, including screenshots of the devices’ menus, sales listings, and user reviews that highlight the presence of thousands of unlicensed games.

The Notorious Markets list, compiled each year by the Office of the United States Trade Representative (USTR), identifies entities that “facilitate the trafficking of counterfeit and pirated goods” and serves as a diplomatic tool to pressure foreign governments to enforce intellectual‑property protections. Inclusion can trigger a range of repercussions, from heightened customs scrutiny to potential sanctions and restrictions on export licenses. While most entries have been web‑based platforms—such as torrent sites, streaming services, and e‑commerce marketplaces—Anbernic’s potential addition would broaden the scope to physical devices, signaling a shift in how authorities view the piracy problem.

Industry analysts note that the retro‑gaming market has exploded in recent years, driven by nostalgia and the scarcity of original hardware. Companies like Anbernic have capitalized on this trend by offering compact, affordable consoles that emulate classic systems and support a wide range of game formats. However, the line between legitimate emulation—where users supply their own legally owned ROMs—and outright piracy has become increasingly blurred. Critics argue that manufacturers who ship devices with pre‑installed, unlicensed games are effectively selling pirated software, whereas supporters claim that many users purchase these consoles for homebrew and legally obtained titles, and that the devices themselves are neutral tools.

Legal experts caution that the outcome of ESA’s request is not predetermined. The USTR typically evaluates evidence and consults with the Department of Commerce before finalising the list, and there is precedent for companies successfully contesting inclusion by demonstrating compliance measures or removing infringing content. Anbernic could respond by issuing firmware updates that strip illegal games, providing a “clean” version of its hardware, or partnering with rights holders to offer licensed titles. Nonetheless, the ESA’s push reflects growing frustration within the gaming industry over the perceived inadequacy of existing enforcement mechanisms against hardware‑based piracy.

If Anbernic is added to the Notorious Markets list, it could set a new benchmark for how regulators address the intersection of hardware and illicit content. The designation would likely compel other retro‑console makers to reassess their product strategies, possibly accelerating a shift toward licensed retro collections or stricter content vetting processes. As the gaming sector continues to grapple with piracy in an increasingly fragmented digital landscape, the case may also prompt lawmakers to consider broader legislative tools that target not just distribution platforms but also the devices that deliver unlicensed media. The coming weeks will reveal whether ESA’s campaign succeeds, and how the industry adapts to a potential expansion of the Notorious Markets framework.
